observations.text: SP executed the instrument descent to the level required for this stage; however, the start of the descent at the published descent point, the power reduction and the penetration turn were taken only after the IP directed each step. Airspeed reached 18 knots above the penetration airspeed and the aircraft was 10 degrees off the published final approach course before the IP directed the correction and flew part of the descent. Marginal performance for the Training Section - independent execution of the penetration sequence is expected to improve on the following sorties.

SP, working from the standardized penetration procedure of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, started the descent at the published descent point without the IP having to direct the sequence. Power reduction and the penetration turn were initiated after two verbal prompts from the IP, so that airspeed reached 15 knots above the penetration airspeed and the deviation from the final approach course reached 8 degrees, at the limit of the allowable deviations. The deviations were recognized and corrected, although with delay, and no IP intervention on the controls was required. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP began the penetration at the published descent point and flew the depicted routing without IP prompting. Small errors in the timing of the power reduction left airspeed 12 knots above the penetration airspeed and produced a maximum deviation of 7 degrees from the final approach course, both recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention. The routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals were not violated. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP executed the descent using the TACAN presentation accurately and quickly according to the standardized procedure, complying with the ATC instructions and the published routing. Airspeed was held within 6 knots of the penetration airspeed and the final approach course within 3 degrees throughout the descent, and the level-off at the published altitude was made without overshoot. No IP intervention or prompting was required. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP applied the penetration procedure flawlessly, anticipating the descent point, the power reduction and the penetration turn, and cross-checking the raw VOR/DME and TACAN picture against the published profile. Deviations remained negligible, with airspeed inside 3 knots of the penetration airspeed and the final approach course held within 1 degree, and the level-off altitude was captured with no correction. Knowledge of the procedure and accuracy of control were above the levels desired for this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to a non-standardized entry into the penetration, did not reduce power and did not extend the speedbrake before starting the descent, and did not begin the descent at the published descent point. The error was not corrected during the descent, with the result that airspeed exceeded the penetration airspeed by 20 knots and the aircraft passed 11 degrees off the final approach course, and the IP had to reduce power and fly part of the descent. Further study of the penetration procedure in the Techniques and Procedures Manual is required.

SP, due to poor workload distribution, with navigation, communication and aircraft control attempted simultaneously, did not monitor the descent against the published routing and did not start the penetration turn at the required point. No correction was attempted, with the result that airspeed passed 20 knots above the penetration airspeed and the aircraft rolled out 12 degrees off the final approach course before the IP took the aircraft and re-established the profile. Shedding of secondary tasks during the penetration requires attention.

SP executed the instrument descent within the standards of the Training Section; however, the power reduction and the penetration turn were initiated only after the IP's verbal prompts on two occasions. Airspeed reached 15 knots above the penetration airspeed and the deviation from the final approach course reached 8 degrees, at the limit of the allowable deviations, and both were recognized with delay. Marginal performance - independence in initiating each step of the penetration is expected to improve over the next instrument sorties.

SP started the descent at the published descent point and set the descent parameters without IP prompting. Minor errors in the rate of power reduction left airspeed 12 knots above the penetration airspeed and the course deviation at 6 degrees, both recognized and corrected in a timely manner without the IP's intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP flew the penetration according to the standardized procedure of the Techniques and Procedures Manual, complying with the ATC instructions and the published routing. Airspeed was held within 7 knots of the penetration airspeed and the final approach course within 4 degrees, and the level-off at the published altitude required no prompting or intervention from the IP. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP executed the penetration flawlessly, anticipating the descent point and cross-checking the DME and altitude relationship against the published profile throughout the descent. Deviations were negligible, with airspeed inside 3 knots of the penetration airspeed and the inbound course held within 1 degree, and the transition to final approach was made with no correction required. Accuracy and speed exceeded the levels desired for this stage of training. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to an incorrect assessment of the descent geometry, did not adjust the rate of descent when the DME and altitude relationship diverged from the published profile and descended below the assigned altitude restriction. The divergence was not identified by the SP, with the result that airspeed reached 22 knots above the penetration airspeed and the IP had to take the aircraft to regain the published profile. Review of the penetration profile in the Instrument Approach Manuals is required before the next instrument sortie.

SP, due to over-reliance on automation that was not fully understood, accepted the flight director steering through the penetration turn without an independent check of the raw TACAN presentation. The divergence from the published final approach course went undetected by the SP, with the result that the aircraft rolled out 12 degrees off the inbound course and 18 knots above the penetration airspeed before the IP intervened and re-established the track. An independent raw-data cross-check during every penetration is required.

SP, due to a late power reduction at the descent point, allowed the airspeed to build during the first part of the penetration and did not use the speedbrake to recover the profile. The excess was recognized only after the IP's verbal prompts, with the result that airspeed reached 15 knots above the penetration airspeed, at the limit of the allowable deviation, before the correction was applied.

SP, due to distraction by radio traffic during the descent, allowed the instrument cross-check to lapse and did not correct the drift from the published final approach course in time. The deviation was recognized and corrected with delay, after two verbal prompts from the IP, with the result that the course deviation reached 8 degrees at the limit of the allowable deviation. Protection of the cross-check while working the radio during the penetration requires attention.

SP executed the instrument descent within the desired standards, starting the descent at the published point and correcting the deviations without IP intervention. However, the power corrections were applied in large steps rather than progressively, and airspeed twice reached 12 knots above the penetration airspeed with a course deviation of 6 degrees before being reduced. Marginal performance for the Training Section - a smoother control of the descent parameters is expected to improve.

SP applied the standardized penetration procedure without error, complying with the ATC instructions and with the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals. Airspeed was held within 8 knots of the penetration airspeed and the final approach course within 4 degrees, and the level-off was made accurately and quickly without any IP intervention. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP anticipated the descent point and the penetration turn, setting power and configuration before they were required and cross-checking the descent continuously against the published DME and altitude profile. Deviations remained negligible, with airspeed inside 3 knots of the penetration airspeed and the inbound course held within 1 degree to the final approach fix. Knowledge of the procedure was flawless and the transition to final approach was faster than required at this stage. Above end of block MIF achieved.

SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the published penetration procedure, could not determine the descent point and the level-off altitudes from the approach plate without assistance and did not start the descent on receipt of the clearance. The IP had to direct the sequence step by step and fly part of the descent, with the result that airspeed exceeded the penetration airspeed by 20 knots and the aircraft was 12 degrees off the final approach course at the transition to final. Further study of the penetration procedure in the Techniques and Procedures Manual and AFMAN 11-202 VOL3 is required.

SP, due to inadequate workload management during the descent phase, did not reassess the published routing after the change of the ATC clearance and did not ask the IP about the restriction that had not been understood. No descent was started at the required point and no correction was attempted, with the result that the aircraft was 14 degrees off the assigned radial and 20 knots above the penetration airspeed when the IP took the aircraft and re-established the published profile. Earlier inquiry toward the IP when a clearance is not understood is required.

SP, due to a late start of the penetration, began the descent well after the published descent point and did not increase the rate of descent to regain the published profile. The divergence was recognized only on the IP's verbal prompt, with the result that airspeed reached 15 knots above the penetration airspeed, at the limit of the allowable deviation, before the correction was made. The correction was then applied correctly, but with delay.

SP, due to an aircraft state that had diverged from the SP's mental model without being reassessed, continued the penetration turn past the computed lead point after the bearing pointer had already indicated the overshoot. The error went undetected until the IP prompted a recheck of the inbound course, with the result that the deviation from the final approach course reached 8 degrees, at the limit of the allowable deviation, and was corrected with delay. Re-establishment of the cross-check after every turn requires attention.

SP, due to a coarse control of power after the penetration turn was completed, allowed the airspeed to drift during the second part of the descent. The deviation was recognized without IP intervention and corrected in a timely manner, with the result that airspeed remained 12 knots above the penetration airspeed and was reduced before the final approach fix.

SP, due to complacency on a penetration flown repeatedly on previous sorties, relaxed the cross-check of the inbound course during the descent and allowed a drift from the published final approach course to develop. The deviation was identified by the SP and corrected without the IP's intervention, with the result that the course deviation reached 7 degrees before it was brought back inside the standard. A continuous cross-check of the inbound course throughout the descent is expected on all penetrations.

SP executed the instrument descent accurately and quickly, complying with the ATC instructions and the published routing and correcting the deviations without IP intervention. However, the accuracy was at the edge of the desired standard, with airspeed twice reaching 10 knots above the penetration airspeed and the course deviation reaching 5 degrees before the corrections took effect. Marginal performance for the Training Section - a more immediate control of the descent parameters is expected to improve.

SP knew and applied the penetration procedure flawlessly, anticipating the descent point, the power reduction and the penetration turn without hesitation. The descent was cross-checked continuously against the published DME and altitude profile, and deviations remained negligible, with airspeed inside 3 knots of the penetration airspeed and the inbound course held within 1 degree. Compliance with the routing and altitude restrictions published in MAIP and the Instrument Approach Manuals was exact, and the transition to final approach required no correction. Above end of block MIF achieved.
